content.text: {"relation":"MATCH","consensus_summary":"The blind consensus reads 'poor, meek, needy' as the anawim: the humble faithful who recognize their dependence on God rather than their own resources, are spiritually receptive, and are promised the kingdom/inheritance (Matt 5:3-5; Ps 37:11; Isa 61:1), with secondary readings emphasizing literal socioeconomic poverty, a remnant community, ethical gentleness, or a christological referent.","book_summary":"The book defines the poor, meek, and needy as those bowed and empty-handed before God, able to receive what the self-sufficient refuse; they hear the gospel and inherit the kingdom. The stated opposite is 'Rich' (i.e., the self-sufficient).","consensus_core_identification":"The humble who acknowledge spiritual poverty and depend wholly on God, and who are therefore receptive to and heirs of God's kingdom — contrasted with the proud and self-sufficient.","book_core_identification":"Those emptied of self-sufficiency before God, receptive to the gospel, who inherit the kingdom — contrasted with the rich/self-sufficient.","core_relation":"EQUIVALENT","extension_relation":"SAME_CASES","boundary_disagreement":"None of substance. The book does not adjudicate the spiritual-versus-socioeconomic tension the consensus flags; its phrasing ('bowed and empty-handed before God,' opposite 'Rich') leans toward the spiritualized humility reading, which is exactly the consensus primary meaning. It neither excludes the materially poor nor adds new cases.","material_contradiction":"None. Both identify the same referent: the humble, God-dependent, receptive people contrasted with the proud/self-sufficient rich.","rationale":"The book's core — receptive humility and dependence before God versus self-sufficiency, culminating in hearing the gospel and inheriting the kingdom — is a compact restatement of the consensus primary meaning (the anawim/'poor in spirit' reading found in all four responses). The 'Opposite: Rich' note mirrors the consensus contrast with the proud and self-sufficient (cf. Rev 3:17 in Response A's ecclesiological alternative and the Lukan woes). Differences are purely in wording and compression; no boundary is redrawn and no cases are reclassified.","citation_support":"STRONG","strongest_objection":"By labeling the opposite simply as 'Rich' and framing the terms wholly as a spiritual posture, the book could be read as flattening the material/socioeconomic dimension that Luke, James 2:5-6, and liberation readings preserve — arguably a narrowing (REFINED). But the consensus itself makes the spiritualized reading primary, and the book's citation of Jas 2:5 and Ps 72:12-13 (literal deliverance of the needy) shows it is not excluding the materially poor; so the objection does not establish a material boundary change.","confidence":"high"}
